coredata.dc:description: Imidazolium-functionalized octaphenyl polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane nanoparticles were incorporated into imidazolium-functionalized poly(ether ether ketone) (ImPEEK) to fabricate high-performance anion exchange membranes with tuneable microphase separation structures and efficient ion transport channels. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy observations revealed the formation of ion channels in the membranes due to the aggregation of imidazolium groups. The transport of hydroxide ions in the composite membranes was facilitated by the increase in the effective ion mobility from 2.27×10−4 to 3.09×10−4 cm2 s−1 V−1, while their hydroxide conductivity at 30°C (36.22–44.11mScm−1) was significantly higher than that of an ImPEEK control membrane (30.66mScm−1).

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Imidazolium-functionalized octaphenyl polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane nanoparticles were incorporated into imidazolium-functionalized poly(ether ether ketone) (ImPEEK) to fabricate high-performance anion exchange membranes with tuneable microphase separation structures and efficient ion transport channels. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy observations revealed the formation of ion channels in the membranes due to the aggregation of imidazolium groups. The transport of hydroxide ions in the composite membranes was facilitated by the increase in the effective ion mobility from 2.27×10−4 to 3.09×10−4 cm2 s−1 V−1, while their hydroxide conductivity at 30°C (36.22–44.11mScm−1) was significantly higher than that of an ImPEEK control membrane (30.66mScm−1).

ce:section.ce:para: Fuel cells are electrochemical devices that directly convert chemical energy to electrical power. The currently known types of fuel cells include polymer electrolyte fuel cells (PEFCs), alkaline fuel cells, solid oxide fuel cells, molten carbonate fuel cells, and phosphoric acid fuel cells [1,2]. Among these types, PEFCs exhibit many attractive properties (such as low operational temperature, compact structure, high power density, and short start-up time), which make them potentially applicable for manufacturing mobile devices, vehicles, and miniature generators [3–5]. Polymer electrolyte membranes are the core components of PEFCs, which play the following two important roles: 1) transporting ions between electrodes to maintain the integrity of the current loop and 2) physically separating oxygen and fuel species between electrodes to avoid a short circuit [6]. Most of the currently used polymer electrolyte membranes are proton exchange membranes (PEMs). However, their drawbacks (including the necessity of using noble metal electrocatalysts and poor oxygen reduction kinetics) dramatically limit the potential applications and commercialization of proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) [7,8]. As an alternative solution, alkaline anion exchange membranes (AEMs) have been developed. In contrast to PEMs, AEMs can be utilized with nonprecious metal-based catalysts (such as Fe, Ni, and Ag) under alkaline conditions [9–11]. Furthermore, the alkaline environment of AEMs promotes the oxygen reduction reaction, which allows the use a larger variety of fuels (including hydrazine) [12–14]. Generally, an AEM must possess high hydroxide conductivity (to ensure a high power density of the fuel cell) and good stability (to ensure its sufficient durability). However, the conductivities of AEMs are typically low due to the low ionic mobility (IM) of hydroxide ions (43% lower than that of protons at infinite dilution and temperature of 25°C) [5,15]. Since IM is an inherent non-tunable property of hydroxide ions, significant efforts have been spent up to date to reinforce the ionic transport characteristics of AEMs.

Generally, the polymers for AEMs consist of hydrophobic backbones (such as poly(phenyl ether) [16,17], poly(aryl ether ketone) [18,19], and poly(aryl ether sulfone) [20–22]) and hydrophilic pendant chains containing conductive groups (such as quaternary amine [22,23], imidazoline [24,25], guanidinium [26,27], and phosphonium [28,29]. The incompatible hydrophilic pendant chains and hydrophobic backbones aggregate into multiple phases to form a thermodynamically steady state. The hydrophilic phases provide a pathway for the ionic transport in AEMs; however, they are usually narrow and branched because the rigidity of the polymer backbones causes less pronounced phase separation and the formation of a dead-end’pocket’ structure, which significantly reduces the efficiency of ionic transport [4,5,30]. Thus, tuning the parameters of microphase separation in AEMs can be effectively used for optimizing their ionic transport properties.

It has been widely established that the introduction of functional fillers into a polymer membrane represents a facile and promising method for tuning the microphase separation properties of ion exchange membranes [24,31–36]. The filler nanoparticles containing high-density modified hydrophilic conductive groups exhibit strong attraction to the hydrophilic pendant chains and strong repulsion to the hydrophobic backbones, which act as’seeds’ guiding the microphase aggregation process at the filler/polymer interface and sequentially generate well-defined channels to promote ion transport, as shown in Fig. 1. For example, the incorporation of ionic liquid-functionalized graphene oxide into a polybenzimidazole matrix increased both the maximum power density and proton conductivity of the composite membrane by a factor of 2 (as compared to that of the pristine membrane) [31]. After nanozirconia particles were incorporated into a quaternized poly(arylene ether sulfone) (QPAES) membrane to produce optimized channels at the nanozirconia/QPAES interface, its hydroxide conductivity was increased by 95.8% [32].

In this study, modified octaphenyl polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (O-POSS) was selected as a novel filler. It represents a hybrid material consisting of inorganic cage-like Si-O cores surrounded by eight phenyl groups, which exhibits the following unique features. 1) The nano-size of O-POSS particles allows precise tuning of the ion channels on the nanoscale. 2) The addition of O-POSS creates a substantial amount of ion channels at the polymer/filler interface due to its large specific surface area. 3) The nanoscale O-POSS can form well-dispersed colloidal particles that prevent the aggregation or sedimentation of composite membranes in the casting solution. Poly(ether ether ketone) (PEEK), an excellent engineering plastic with good mechanical strength, high oxidation resistance, and good chemical stability, was utilized as the polymer matrix. In particular, PEEK exhibits superior alkaline stability and thus can be stored in 50% NaOH solution at a temperature of about 126.7°C for several weeks. Imidazolium group was selected as a conductive group due to its low cost and high conductivity. Hence, imidazolium-functionalized O-POSS was incorporated into imidazolium-functionalized poly(ether ether ketone) (ImPEEK) in this work to prepare composite membranes with superior electrochemical properties. The morphology of the produced ion channels was examined by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) techniques, while the electrical characteristics of the composite membranes were studied by measuring their hydroxide conductivity. The ion transport properties of the fabricated membranes were optimized by analysing the effective ionic mobility (EIM) of hydroxide ions inside the membrane. In addition, other chemical-mechanical properties of the composite membranes were also systematically investigated, including their alkaline, thermal, and physical stabilities as well as water uptakes and swelling areas.

Anhydrous zinc chloride (ZnCl2, analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), dichloromethane (DCM, analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE, analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), 1-methylimidazole (analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), and dimethyl formamide (DMF, analytical reagent, 99.9wt%) were provided by J&K Scientific Ltd. O-POSS (analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), n-octanol (analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), paraformaldehyde (analytical reagent, 99.9wt%), and N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, analytical reagent, 99.9wt%) were provided by Shanghai Aladdin Reagent Ltd. Concentrated sulfuric acid (con. H2SO4, analytical reagent, 98.2wt%), concentrated hydrochloric acid (con. HCl, analytical reagent, about 12M) and sodium hydroxide standard solution (stand. NaOH, acidimetric standard, 2M/1M/0.1M/0.01M) were provided by Tianjin Guangfu Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. Chloromethyl octyl ether (CMOE, DCM solution) was synthesized using the procedure reported in Ref. [4]. Chloromethyl methyl ether (CMME, analytical reagent, 99.0wt%) was provided by Chengdu Ai Keda Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. PEEK (450PF) was provided by Victrex© (England). All materials and chemicals not mentioned above were of analytical grade. Deionized water was used throughout the entire study.

PEEK was chloromethylated in the following four steps. 1) PEEK (8g) was stirred in con. H2SO4 (480mL) for 4h to ensure its complete dissolution. The reaction temperature was maintained at a level of −10±2°C to avoid undesired side reactions. 2) CMOE (160mL) was added to the PEEK solution, and the reaction temperature was maintained at −10±2°C for 20min. 3) The obtained orange solution was added to excess water to precipitate the chloromethylated PEEK (CmPEEK). 4) The crude CmPEEK powder was washed by water and ethanol, dissolved in NMP (8−10wt%), and then reprecipitated in ethanol.

O-POSS was chloromethylated in the following four steps. 1) O-POSS (1g) and ZnCl2 (1.06g) were dispersed in DCM (42mL) followed by the slow addition of the mixture of 24mL CMME and 30mL DCM. The reaction temperature was maintained at 50°C for 24h. 2) Water (300mL) was added to quench the chloromethylation reaction, and the organic phase was separated using a separatory funnel. 3) The organic phase was washed with excess water until all ZnCl2 and CMME species were extracted. 4) The organic phase was evaporated using a rotary evaporator to obtain the white powder of chloromethylated O-POSS (Cm-O-POSS).

A solution-casting method and the Menshutkin reaction were used to fabricate composite membranes in situ in the following four steps. 1) Cm-O-POSS (or O-POSS) (y g, y < 0.6) was dispersed in 1-methylimidazole (10 y mL), and CmPEEK (x g, x = 0.6−y) was dissolved in 1-methylimidazole (10x mL). The Cm-O-POSS (or O-POSS) suspension was ultrasonicated for 24h, and the CmPEEK solution was stirred for 24h. 2) The CmPEEK solution was mixed with the Cm-O-POSS suspension and then stirred at 25°C for 24h. 3) The obtained mixture was cast on a clear glass plate and then successively dried at 40°C for 12h, 60°C for 24h, and 80°C for 6h. According to the Menshutkin reaction, CmPEEK and Cm-O-POSS were completely converted into ImPEEK and Im-O-POSS after this step, respectively. 4) The obtained membrane with a thickness of 70±2.5µm was peeled off from the glass and immersed in 1.0M stand. NaOH solution for 12h. After that, the membrane was washed with water until the rinse solution became neutral and dried at 25°C under vacuum. The produced composite membranes were named ImPEEK/ImP-X and ImPEEK/P-X, where /ImP or /P represented the utilized filler (Im-O-POSS or O-POSS), and X denoted the weight ratio of the filler to the entire membrane (X=x/(x+y)).

To conduct 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) measurements, a polymer sample (0.025g) was dissolved in 1mL of deuterium dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO-d6) and then tested using a 600MHz NMR instrument (Inova600, Varian Ltd., USA). The composite membrane samples (0.25g) were dissolved in 10mL of DMSO-d6 and centrifuged at a speed of 10,000 r/min for 60min to separate the Im-O-POSS phase from the mixture. The supernatant liquid was examined using the 600MHz NMR instrument to investigate the conversion of CMPEEK to ImPEEK. Due to the insolubility of CM-POSS and Im-POSS in all deuterated reagents, solid state 13C NMR was employed to probe their chemical structure using a 600MHz solid-state NMR instrument.

To perform HRTEM observations, a powder sample (0.05g) was dispersed in ethanol (1.00mL), loaded onto a copper grid, and dried at a temperature of 60°C. The membrane sample was stained with 29.4mmolL−1 chloroauric acid for 24h, cut to form ultramicrocuts with thicknesses of 70nm, and loaded onto the copper grid. The operating voltage, current, and vacuum background pressure of the HRTEM instrument (2010F, JEOL Ltd., Japan) were 200kV, 100 μA, and 1.4×10−6 Pa, respectively. The operating mode was a bright tilt one. To conduct scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations, a membrane sample was broken in liquid nitrogen, and its cross-sections were coated with Au before testing. The operating voltage, current, and vacuum background pressure of the SEM instrument (S-4800, Hitachi Ltd., Japan) were 25kV, 100mA, and 1.4×10−4 Pa, respectively.

To perform SAXS measurements, the membrane sample with an area of 1×3cm2 was fixed onto a sample holder and studied using a D/max-2500/PC X-ray diffractometer (RIGAKU Co., Ltd., Japan). The 2θ angle ranged from 0.25° to 5.25°, and the scanning rate was 0.25°min−1.

The alkaline stabilities of AEMs are typically low due to the easy degradation of their cation groups (such as quaternary ammonium and imidazolium ones). While this study aimed at the development of a suitable approach to increasing the hydroxide conductivities of AEMs by optimizing the parameters of the microphase separation process, the proposed method should not deteriorate their alkaline stabilities. In this work, the membrane samples were stirred in excess 2M NaOH solution at 60°C for 144h, during which their hydroxide conductivities were periodically measured every 12h (since residual hydroxide conductivity could potentially affect the alkaline stability of a membrane).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Chloromethylation and imidazolium functionalization of PEEK and O-POSS
ce:section.ce:para: The chloromethylated PEEK was characterized by 1H NMR (see Fig. 2(a)). The peak at 4.7ppm corresponds to the α-hydrogens of the benzyl chloride groups of CmPEEK [4,25]. According to the area ratio of hydrogen atoms, the functionalization degree (FD) of CmPEEK is 61.8%. In Fig. 2(b), the peak at 4.7ppm is shifted to 5.6ppm, indicating the full conversion of chloromethyl species to methylimidazolium ones. In addition, the new peak observed at 3.6ppm is related to the methyl groups of methylimidazolium moieties, which further confirms successful imidazolium functionalization. For O-POSS, the peak at 46ppm in Fig. 2(c) originates from the chloromethyl carbons of the benzene ring, indicating successful chloromethylation of O-POSS. In Fig. 2(d), the peak detected at 46ppm is shifted to 60ppm, and a new peak corresponding to the methyl species of methylimidazolium groups appears at 36ppm. The obtained results indicate that Cm-O-POSS has been fully converted to Im-O-POSS. However, due to the strong nuclear Overhauser effect, it is hard to quantitatively determine the FD of Cm-O-POSS via 13C NMR. The FD of Cm-O-POSS (35.5%) was calculated from its X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy data (Fig. S1). Since each O-POSS molecule contains eight modifiable benzene rings (in contrast to only one benzene ring existing in a PEEK unit), the FD of Cm-O-POSS is relatively high.

The obtained IEC values are listed in Table 1. The IEC of the ImPEEK membrane is 1.43mmolg−1. Owing to the high IEC of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles (2.01mmolg−1), the IEC of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membrane was elevated relatively high. In contrast, the IEC of the ImPEEK/P-X membrane was significantly reduced because the corresponding O-POSS species contained no conductive groups.

The HRTEM images of O-POSS and Im-O-POSS particles are shown in Fig. 3(b) and (c), respectively (the image of the blank copper grid is depicted in Fig. 3(a) for comparison purposes). The diameters of uniform O-POSS nanoparticles range between 2.0 and 2.5nm and are larger than the calculated size of a single O-POSS molecule (1.666nm across the diagonal; the utilized calculation method is described in the Supplementary Material section), indicating the formation of multiple O-POSS aggregates. After imidazolium functionalization, the diameter of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles increased to 3.0−3.5nm due to the introduction of pendant groups.

The general morphology of the membranes was examined by probing their cross-sections (
Fig. 4(a)–(f)). The obtained ImPEEK/ImP-X composite membranes appear very homogeneous without any obvious defects because the presence of imidazolium groups on the Im-O-POSS surface increased the compatibility between Im-O-POSS and ImPEEK species. In contrast, the incorporation of O-POSS (Fig. 4(d)–(f)) decreased the homogeneity of membranes, inducing the formation of defects. Moreover, the uniform distribution of Im-O-POSS particles was further confirmed via HRTEM observations ( Fig. 6) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy mapping (Fig. S2).

The nanoscale structures of membranes were examined by SAXS and HRTEM, as shown in Figs. 5 and 6, respectively. The SAXS pattern recorded for ImPEEK contains no apparent peaks in the scattering vector (q, q = 4π sinθ λ−1) range of 0.40−3.33nm−1, indicating poor microphase separation. After the incorporation of Im-O-POSS particles, a peak at around 0.73nm−1 was observed, which gradually shifted to 0.61nm−1 with an increase in the Im-O-POSS content (during this process, the peak intensity gradually increased as well). The observed phenomenon indicates the formation of microphase separation structures and related regular ion channels inside the membranes, while the peak shift suggests the continuous expansion of these channels with increasing filler content and, therefore, effective incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles.

During the HRTEM studies (Fig. 6(a)–(d)), the membranes were stained with chloroauric acid, sliced by a microtome, and loaded onto a copper grid before testing (chloroauric acid strongly interacts with alkaline imidazolium groups, but not with hydrophobic polymer chains). Since Au is a relatively heavy metal, it can significantly interfere with the operating electrons of HRTEM. Consequently, the dark regions in the HRTEM images likely correspond to the conductive hydrophilic phases of the membranes. Fig. S3 shows a comparison between the HRTEM images of the stained and non-stained membranes, which confirms the effectiveness and necessity of the staining procedure. The ImPEEK control membrane does not exhibit a distinct microphase separation, and its hydrophilic and hydrophobic phases are narrow and chaotic. In contrast, the ImPEEK/ImP-X composite membranes contain the enhanced microphase separation structures. The addition of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles successfully induced the aggregation of imidazolium groups to form hydrophilic clusters with diameters about 4−5nm, which sequentially acted as efficient springboards with low resistances facilitating the transport of hydroxide ions inside the membrane. When the filler content increased to 20%, the ion clusters remained homogeneously dispersed and adhered to each other to form continuous pathways. In contrast, the incorporation of O-POSS particles inhibited the formation of microphase separation structures. The bright dots depicted in Fig. 6(b) denote the bulk non-conductive hydrophobic phases resulting from the severe aggregation of nonpolar O-POSS species.
The obtained results demonstrate that the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles successfully tailored the membrane microstructure, leading to the formation of conductive ion channels.

According to Fig. 7(a), the area swellings of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes are larger than that of the ImPEEK control membrane across the entire temperature range, which can be attributed to their higher IEC values. However, the area swellings remained in the acceptable range and was below 9% at 30°C and below 25% at 60°C. In contrast, the area swellings of the ImPEEK/P-X membranes were higher in the entire temperature range despite their low values of IECs. Such deteriorative swelling was caused by the incorporation of incompatible O-POSS particles, which disturbed the hydrophobic phase of the membranes and negatively affected their physical stability. Similarly, the water uptakes of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes (Fig. 7(b)) were higher than that of ImPEEK, while the water uptakes of the ImPEEK/P-X membranes were higher than the magnitudes measured for the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes with the same filler contents.

Hydroxide conductivity is a major parameter of AEMs [5,15,37]. As shown in Fig. 8(a), the conductivities of all membranes exhibit positive correlation with temperature, and the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles significantly increases the hydroxide conductivity of the studied membranes from 30.66 to 44.11 mS cm−1 at 30°C (their chloride conductivities are characterized in Fig. S9). In addition, the Arrhenius plots depicted in Fig. 8(b) reveal that the incorporation of Im-O-POSS particles decreases the activation energy of the hydroxide ion transfer process (Ea) in the studied membranes ( Table 2), and that the magnitude of Ea is further decreased with increasing filler content. This phenomenon indicates fast and low-resistant transfer of hydroxide ions inside the membrane, and thus the successful formation of efficient ion channels. In order to provide an insight into the effect of the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles on the hydroxide conductivities of membranes, additional studies were performed. The hydroxide conductivity of a membrane is governed by the two factors (IECv and EIM) according to Eq. (7) [4,5,15,25,38,39]:
(7)
σ = F a μ
where σ (S cm−1) is the hydroxide conductivity (mS cm−1), F is the Faraday's constant, a (mmolcm−3) is the IECv, and μ (cm2 s−1 V−1) is the EIM of hydroxide ions inside the membrane.

The unit of IECv is the number of moles of hydroxide ions per a unit volume, which reflects the amount of transported charge carriers (ion exchange groups). The IECv values of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes (Fig. 8(c)) are slightly higher than that of ImPEEK at low temperatures because of the higher IECm values (see Table 1). In contrast, the incorporation of O-POSS nanoparticles not only reduces the IECm values of membranes, but also increases their swellings. Thus, the IECv values of the ImPEEK/P-X membranes were significantly lower than those of the other membranes. The effective mobility is the velocity of hydroxide ions in the direction across the membranes, which reflects the combined effects of the IM of charge carriers and channel morphology (such as the tortuosity of ion channels, number of channels, and spatial proximity of ionic groups). Significantly, the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles substantially increases the EIMs of the membranes (Fig. 8(d)). For instance, the EIM of ImPEEK is 2.26×10−4 cm2 s−1 V−1, and those of ImPEEK/ImP-X at 30°C are between 2.63×10−4 and 3.09×10−4 cm2 s−1 V−1. The increased EIMs correspond to larger velocities of hydroxide ions across the membranes, which result from the formation of efficient ion channels by the incorporated Im-O-POSS particles. The EIMs of all membranes increase with increasing temperature, which can be attributed to the following two factors. 1) The IM of hydroxide ions is positively correlated with temperature. 2) The swellings of membranes broaden their ionic pathways and open up the dead-end’pocket’ structures. Fig. 8(e) illustrates the correlation between the IECv and EIM parameters. The EIM exhibits a negative correlation with IECv because the IM of hydroxide ions is negatively correlated with the ionic concentration. However, the EIMs of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes are higher than that of the ImPEEK membrane when their corresponding values of IECv are similar (see the vertical imaginary line in the figure). Moreover, the IECv magnitudes of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes are higher than those of the ImPEEK/P-X membranes at similar values of EIM (see the horizontal imaginary line in the figure). The observed phenomenon further confirms that the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles can optimize the morphology of channels to form efficient ionic pathways.

The methanol permeabilities of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes were examined in order to evaluate their potential applicability for direct methanol fuel cells (see Fig. 9(a)). The highly efficient ion channels formed by the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles can act not only as ion transport pathways, but also as methanol transport pathways. As a result, the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes exhibit higher methanol permeabilities (8.86×10−7−9.39×10−7 cm2 s−1) as compared to that of the ImPEEK control membrane (8.08×10−7 cm2 s−1). In contrast, the incorporation of O-POSS particles disturbs the ImPEEK channels, thus decreasing their methanol permeability. Membrane selectivity (defined as the ratio of the hydroxide conductivity to the methanol permeability) was utilized in this work to evaluate the overall performance of the studied membranes (Fig. 9(b)). The ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes exhibit higher selectivities as compared to those of the ImPEEK control membrane and ImPEEK/P-X membranes. In addition, the methanol permeabilities of the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes varied around 10−7. The obtained results combined with the hydroxide conductivity values demonstrate significant application potential of the ImPEEK/ImP-X composite membranes for fuel cells.

In this work, a new approach to the formation of highly efficient ion channels in AEMs is proposed. Im-O-POSS nanoparticles were utilized to induce the aggregation of conductive groups inside the ImPEEK membranes. The results of SAXS and HRTEM measurements showed that the ImPEEK/ImP-X membranes exhibited well-defined microstructures, while the data obtained via ionic mobility analysis revealed that the incorporation of Im-O-POSS nanoparticles promoted fast ion transport in the highly efficient ion channels. As a result, the produced composite membranes exhibited high hydroxide conductivities (up to 85.3 mS cm−1), which were much higher than the value obtained for the ImPEEK control membrane.
